newsitem.title: USA: U.S. sees less chlamydia among young women.
newsitem.headline: U.S. sees less chlamydia among young women.

text.p: Cases of chlamydia, one of the most common and serious sexually transmitted diseases, have dropped substantially in states where women are being screened and treated, federal health officials said Thursday.

The Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) said positive tests for chlamydia among women under age 20 have fallen by 16 to 31 percent since screening and treatment programmes began in 11 states and the District of Columbia in 1994.

Most cases of chlamydia go undiagnosed, untreated and unreported because the disease usually has no symptoms. It was the nation's most commonly reported infectious disease during 1995, with 477,638 cases reported to the CDC.
If left untreated in women, chlamydia can lead to pelvis inflammatory disease, infertility and potentially fatal tubal pregnancy, the agency said.

"Chlamydia screening and treatment should be a standard of care for sexually active adolescents and young adults," said Dr. Judith Wasserheit of the CDC's Division of Sexually Transmitted Diseases Prevention.

"Providers must make this a routine part of preventive health care for at-risk patients, and sexually active adolescents and young adults should discuss chlamydia screening with their providers," Wasserheit said.

The CDC estimated that more than 3-1/2 million cases of chlamydia go undiagnosed every year. Untreated chlamydia infections and complications cost the nation more than $2 billion in 1994, the agency said.
